newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania eyes $700 million deal with Canada's AECL.
newsitem.headline: Romania eyes $700 million deal with Canada's AECL.

text.p: Romania hopes to sign a $700 million accord with a Canadian-led corsortium this year to complete a second reactor at the country's sole nuclear power station, the plant's director said on Friday.
"We hope to complete the negotiations and sign the deal this autumn with Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd (AECL)," Cristian Talmozan told Reuters.
He made the remarks during a visit by Moldovan Prime Minister Ion Ciubuc at the plant, 200 km (125 miles) east of Bucharest on the River Danube.

The first of five 700-megawatt reactors planned at Cernavoda, a project started under late dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, came on stream last April and supplies about 10 percent of Romania's electricity output.

Officials say the second reactor is about 40 percent complete. Talmozan said AECL executives were expected to start final negotiations with the Renel RA electricity authority on the $700 million project next week.

"During preliminary talks our share was set at $350 million. We must identify sources to finance our part of the programme," he said. "It will be difficult to get the funds, but I'm optimistic about the outcome of the talks with AECL."
The Cernavoda plant is the first in eastern Europe to use a Western reactor, Canadian-developed Candu technology, built together with Italy's Ansaldo Spa.

With some 16 years required to complete the first reactor and around $10 billion spent on infrastructure, casings and equipment, Cernavoda was probably the biggest of Ceausescu's grandiose industrial schemes.
The centrist government has set the plant's extension as a priority for the next five years to fight declining crude oil and gas reserves and cut fuel imports.
"Based on our experience with the first reactor, I think we could start the second one by the year 2001," said Viorel Marculescu, director of the second reactor.

After Ceausescu's overthrow in the December 1989 revolution, Romania had difficulty financing completion of the first reactor and a 1990 survey revealed that part of the equipment was in poor condition and the welding was faulty.
But after five years of intense work under Western supervision, international experts have described the reactor's operations as excellent.

Talmozan said he believed Moldova, heavily dependent on Russia and other ex-Soviet republics for its energy imports, could be persuaded to shoulder part of the costs of the second reactor in exchange for power supplies.
But Ciubuc said cash-strapped Moldova, sandwiched between Romania and Ukraine, had no immediate investment plans.
